48: flops? It means you probably don’t have anything the times that you check-raise. This makes it difficult for you to check-raise as a bluff. It also means that Villain can bet over 70% of his hands and get away with it. Villain c-bets and you’re often forced to fold when you miss. He can bet with impunity and you can’t really do anything to change that. Truly, the only incentive you have to flat out of position is pot odds.

I say ‘usually’ because this is where the power of position comes into play. It’s easy to think that all you have to do is estimate Villain’s stealing range, plug that into a pre-flop equity calculator, and compare that equity to your pot odds. The problem is that you won’t always be able to realize all of your equity by flatting.

Pre-flop equity calculators assume that you will see all five cards. But now you know that you will rarely see all five cards since I’ve established that Villain can bet over 70% of his range with impunity on most boards. Consider the times you defend with a hand like 8-7o on the same board of J-6-2r. You check, Villain bets, and you have nothing so you fold.

You lost an opportunity to make a pair against a hand like K-Q. You also lost an opportunity for the turn and river to run out 10-9, 9-5, 5-4, 8-8, 7-7, or 8-7 against a hand like A-J. You missed these opportunities because by flatting you acknowledged that your range was weaker than Villain’s range. This all leads back to my initial point. Flatting is bad and limping is worse. So always consider the four ways that you can create profit pre-flop: card edge, skill edge, position, and initiative.

After finishing an AAS in Paramedic Technology – most of which was at a Level I trauma center – I’m now used to things like protocols, guidelines, quality assurance programs, and decentralized command concepts. It’s easy to get distracted by a broken leg while someone is going into cardiac arrest. You have to prioritize.

Protocols are for situations that come up frequently. Guidelines are for situations on the fringe of protocols. Quality assurance programs are for developing the critical thinking skills necessary to solve problems outside the protocols and guidelines.
